title: Research Bite #71: Marked Pedagogies: Examining Linguistic Biases in Personalized Automated Writing Feedback
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #71 covers Mei Tan, Lena Phalen, and Dorottya Demszky's 'Marked Pedagogies: Examining Linguistic Biases in Personalized Automated Writing Feedback,' published in the Proceedings of the LAK26: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (2026). The researchers held 600 American eighth-grade persuasive essays from the public PERSUADE dataset completely constant and asked four widely used LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo, and two Llama models) to generate feedback while only varying the student attributes named in the prompt -- race, gender, motivation level, and learning needs like English-learner or disability status. Because the essay text itself never changed, any difference in feedback could only be attributed to the model's assumptions about the labeled student. The result was systematic, stereotype-aligned bias: feedback for students marked by race, language status, or disability skewed toward more praise, less substantive critique, and lower assumed ability, with a focus on surface corrections rather than engaging with the student's ideas. The authors term this pattern 'Marked Pedagogies' -- personalization that quietly reproduces social stereotypes rather than genuinely adapting to need.
points: The controlled design (identical essay text, only the labeled student attribute varies) makes this some of the cleanest available evidence that LLM feedback bias is driven by demographic assumptions, not by anything in the actual writing.

The specific bias pattern -- more praise, less substantive critique, lower assumed ability for marked groups -- means AI 'personalization' can function as a subtle form of lowered expectations, delivered at scale and dressed up as individualized support.

Testing across four different widely used models (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo, two Llama variants) shows this is not one vendor's idiosyncratic quirk but a pattern that recurs across the current generation of commercially deployed LLMs.

Schools adopting AI writing-feedback tools for equity or scale reasons should treat this finding as a direct warning: without auditing, 'personalized' feedback may systematically shortchange exactly the students it claims to serve better.

The 'Marked Pedagogies' framing is itself a useful diagnostic concept for teachers reviewing any AI tool's output: check whether feedback substance (not just tone) changes when the same work is attributed to different student profiles.

The researchers took 600 American eighth-grade persuasive essays from the public PERSUADE dataset and asked four widely used models (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo, and two Llama models) to give feedback, varying only the student attributes named in the prompt: race, gender, motivation, and learning needs such as English language learner or learning disability status.
The essay text never changed. Comparing the language across conditions, they found systematic, stereotype-aligned shifts.

Feedback for students marked by race, language, or disability tended towards more praise, less substantive critique, and assumptions of limited ability, focusing on surface corrections rather than ideas. The authors call these patterns 'Marked Pedagogies.'

AI writing tools don't treat every student the same. Tell a model that a student is low-achieving, an English language learner, or from a particular racial group, and its feedback shifts in stereotyped ways: more praise, less substantive critique, even when the writing is word-for-word identical.
